# End-of-Service Gratuity Under Jordanian Law

End-of-service gratuity is a benefit paid to a worker when their employment ends, calculated differently depending on whether the worker is covered by the Social Security Law.

## For workers NOT subject to the Social Security Law

**Labour Law 1996, Article 32** sets the basic rule: end-of-service remuneration is **one month's wage for each year of actual service**. For partial years, the worker receives proportional remuneration. 

The calculation is based on **the last wage received during the period of employment**. However, if all or part of the wage is calculated on commission or task work, the remuneration is instead calculated on **the average of the monthly wage received during the twelve months preceding the end of service**. If the service period is less than twelve months, **the monthly average of the total service period is used instead**.

Importantly, **intermissions (breaks) between jobs not exceeding sixty days are counted as uninterrupted employment** when calculating the remuneration.

## For workers subject to the Social Security Law

**Social Security Law, Article 102(a)** states that the employer's obligations under the Old-Age, Disability and Death Insurance provisions **replace the statutory end-of-service indemnity** under the Labour Law.

However, **Social Security Law, Article 103(a)** protects workers who have better entitlements: if a worker's bylaws, arrangements, or collective agreements provide better financial rights than the Social Security end-of-service indemnity, the worker retains those vested rights. The employer must pay the difference between the superior contractual rights and what the worker receives from Social Security contributions.

For end-of-service periods **before the Social Security Law came into force**, **Social Security Law, Article 102(b)** requires the employer to pay the end-of-service indemnity and other due rights under the prior law at the time of service termination.

# End-of-Service Gratuity Under Jordanian Law

**What it is and who receives it:**

End-of-service gratuity (also called end-of-service remuneration or indemnity) is a lump-sum payment made to a worker when their employment ends, for any reason. The law that applies depends on whether the worker is covered by the Social Security Law.

---

## Workers NOT covered by Social Security Law

**Eligibility:** Any worker not subject to the Social Security Law whose service ends for any reason.

**Calculation:**
- **Rate:** One month's wage for each year of actual service.
- **Partial years:** For periods less than one full year, the worker receives a proportional remuneration.
- **Wage basis:** Calculated on the last wage received during employment.
- **Exception for commission/task work:** If all or part of the wage is based on commission or task work, use the average monthly wage received during the twelve months before the end of service. If service was shorter than twelve months, use the average of the entire service period.
- **Gaps in service:** Intermissions between jobs not exceeding 60 days are counted as continuous employment when calculating remuneration.

(Labour Law 1996, Article 32)

---

## Workers covered by Social Security Law

**What replaces it:** The employer's obligations under Old-Age, Disability and Death Insurance under the Social Security Law replace the statutory end-of-service indemnity under the Labour Law.

(Social Security Law, Article 102(a))

**Lump Sum Compensation instead:** Insured workers who do not meet conditions for a Retirement or Disability Pension receive a Lump Sum Compensation calculated as follows:

**If employment ends due to death or natural disability, or completion of age 60 (male) or 55 (female), without meeting pension conditions:**
- Rate: 15% of the average monthly wage for the last 24 contributions, or the average monthly wage multiplied by the number of contributions if fewer than 24 contributions exist.

(Social Security Law, Article 70(a))

**If employment ends while under age 60 (male) or 55 (female) because the person no longer meets coverage conditions:**
- If contributions are 120 or fewer: 10% of total wage subject to deduction.
- If contributions are more than 120 but fewer than 216: 12% of total wage subject to deduction.
- If contributions are 216 or more: 15% of total wage subject to deduction.

(Social Security Law, Article 70(b)(1)–(3))

**Better contractual rights retained:** If a worker has a collective agreement, bylaw, or arrangement that provides better financial rights than the statutory end-of-service indemnity, they retain those rights, and the employer must pay the difference between the contractual amount and what the worker must contribute to Social Security.

(Social Security Law, Article 103(a))

# End-of-Service Gratuity: Definition and Calculation

End-of-service gratuity is a payment made to a worker when their employment ends, intended to compensate for their service. How it is calculated depends on whether the worker is covered by the Social Security Law.

## Workers Not Subject to the Social Security Law

Under **Labour Law 1996, Article 32**, a worker not subject to the Social Security Law is entitled to end-of-service remuneration at the rate of **one month's wage for each year of actual service**. For parts of a year, the worker receives proportional remuneration.

The remuneration is calculated on the basis of the **last wage received during the period of employment**. However, if all or part of the wage is calculated on a commission or task-work basis, the remuneration is calculated instead based on the **average of the monthly wage received during the twelve months preceding the end of service**. If the period of service does not reach twelve months, the **monthly average of the total service period** is used instead.

**Intermissions between jobs not exceeding sixty days are counted as uninterrupted employment** when calculating the remuneration.

## Workers Subject to the Social Security Law

Under **Social Security Law, Article 102(a)**, the employer's obligations regarding Old-Age, Disability and Death Insurance **replace the statutory end-of-service indemnity under the Labour Law**.

The amount depends on the worker's age and contribution record:

**Social Security Law, Article 70(a)**: If employment ends due to death or natural disability, or because the worker completes age 60 (male) or 55 (female) or above without qualifying for a Retirement or Disability Pension, the insured or beneficiaries receive a **lump sum compensation at the rate of 15% of the average monthly wage for the last 24 contributions**, or the average monthly wage multiplied by the number of contributions if fewer than 24 contributions have been made.

**Social Security Law, Article 70(b)**: If service ends before age 60 (male) or 55 (female) because the worker no longer meets coverage conditions, compensation is apportioned based on contribution history:
- **10%** of total wages subject to deduction if contributions are 120 or fewer
- **12%** of total wages subject to deduction if contributions are more than 120 but fewer than 216
- **15%** of total wages subject to deduction if contributions are 216 or more

## Retention of Better Rights

Under **Social Security Law, Article 103(a)**, workers retain vested rights under bylaws, arrangements, or collective agreements if those provide better financial benefits than the end-of-service indemnity under the Labour Law. Employers must pay the difference between those rights and contributions to the Social Security Corporation at the end of service. Workers entitled to full end-of-service indemnity under such agreements retain that right in full.

If your period of service has not yet completed a full year, you are entitled to leave with pay proportionate to the duration you have actually worked during that year (Labour Law 1996, Article 61(b)).

You are entitled to **14 days of paid annual leave per year of service**. If you complete **5 consecutive years of service with the same employer**, this rises to **21 days per year** (Labour Law 1996, Article 61(a)).

The documents do not state your years of service, so I cannot tell you which figure applies to your situation. If you've been with your current employer for 5 or more consecutive years, the answer is 21 days; otherwise, it is 14 days.

Additional rules that affect how you use this leave:

- If your service does not complete a full year, you are entitled to a proportionate number of days (Labour Law 1996, Article 61(b)).
- Annual leave may be deferred by agreement to the next year, but your right to deferred leave expires if that year passes without you requesting it (Labour Law 1996, Article 61(c)).
- If leave is divided, no portion may be less than 2 days at a time (Labour Law 1996, Article 62).
- You cannot waive or forfeit your annual leave by agreement (Labour Law 1996, Article 64).
- If your employment ends before you use all your leave, you are entitled to cash payment for unused days (Labour Law 1996, Article 63).

answer:
Your entitlement to paid annual leave depends on how long you have worked for your current employer.

**If you have less than 5 consecutive years of service** with the same employer, you are entitled to **14 days of paid annual leave per year** (Labour Law 1996, Article 61(a)).

**If you have 5 or more consecutive years of service** with the same employer, you are entitled to **21 days of paid annual leave per year**, provided an agreement has been reached for this longer period (Labour Law 1996, Article 61(a)).

If your period of service has not yet completed a full year, you are entitled to paid leave proportionate to the time you have actually worked during that year (Labour Law 1996, Article 61(b)).

Official holidays, religious holidays, and weekends do not count toward your annual leave entitlement (Labour Law 1996, Article 61(a)). If you take your leave in separate periods rather than all at once, no single period can be shorter than 2 days (Labour Law 1996, Article 62). You cannot waive any of your annual leave entitlement—any agreement to do so is void (Labour Law 1996, Article 64).

If your employment ends before you have used all your annual leave, you must be paid in cash for the unused days (Labour Law 1996, Article 63).
